parsed_output.evidence:
Root cause / sink: Expand.java `extractFile(File srcF, File dir, InputStream, String entryName, Date, boolean)` — specifically `File f = FileUtils.resolveFile( dir, entryName );` at Expand.java:153, which calls FileUtils.resolveFile (FileUtils.java:1367-1394, `new File(...)` at 1383) with no post-resolution check that `f` is contained within `dir`. `entryName` is fully attacker-controlled: it comes straight from `ze.getName()` (Expand.java:116) inside `expandFile()`'s ZipInputStream loop, i.e. from the bytes of a zip file that is untrusted input whenever Expand (or any caller of it, e.g. an unarchiving/unwar/unjar task) is used to extract a third-party or user-supplied archive — that zip-content-to-filesystem-path boundary is the trust boundary being crossed. The unchecked File `f` produced at line 153 is then used at FOUR distinct sink call sites in extractFile(), all reachable from the same unchecked resolution and all needing to be covered by a complete fix:
  1. Expand.java:178 — `fos = new FileOutputStream( f );` (arbitrary file write/overwrite outside dest) — exercised directly by this POV.
  2. Expand.java:164-165 — `File dirF = f.getParentFile(); dirF.mkdirs();` (arbitrary directory creation outside dest).
  3. Expand.java:169 — `f.mkdirs();` for zip directory entries (arbitrary directory creation outside dest via a directory-type entry, e.g. name ending in "/../").
  4. Expand.java:204 — `f.setLastModified( entryDate.getTime() );` (arbitrary timestamp tampering on a file outside dest, and also usable purely as an existence/timestomp oracle even without content control).
All four sinks share the identical unguarded source-to-sink path: ZipEntry.getName() (116) → entryName (148) → FileUtils.resolveFile(dir, entryName) (153) → f used at 164/169/178/204.
parsed_output.expected_vulnerable_behavior: On unpatched code, Expand.execute() extracts a zip entry named "../pwned.txt" into a file located one directory ABOVE the supplied destination directory, i.e. outside the intended extraction root. The POV verifies this by checking that the marker-content file exists at the escaped path (parent of dest) after extraction, and prints "VULNERABLE: ..." then exits 0. If the traversal is blocked (patched code throws, or the resolved path is confined to dest), the marker file is absent at the escaped path, the POV prints "SAFE: ..." and exits 1.
parsed_output.notes: The alert contains four traces that all share one root cause (unchecked FileUtils.resolveFile(dir, entryName) result at Expand.java:153) fanning out to four sinks at Expand.java lines 178, 164/169, and 204. I targeted the FileOutputStream write sink (line 178) for the primary POV because it gives the cleanest, most unambiguous, deterministic evidence: a real file with attacker-chosen content lands on disk outside the destination directory, verifiable by simple existence+content checks without relying on timing or filesystem metadata. I validated the POV's discriminating power by temporarily patching Expand.java in this worktree with a canonical-path containment check (dir.getCanonicalPath()-prefix guard before the try block), confirming the same command flips from exit 0 (vulnerable) to exit 1 (blocked), then reverted the product file back to its original unpatched state (verified via `git status --porcelain` showing only the new `.security-pipeline/` directory as untracked, no modifications to tracked files). The other three sinks (164/169 mkdirs, 204 setLastModified) are not separately exercised by this POV but are documented in `evidence`/`regression_hint` so the patcher does not fix only the write path.

parsed_output.regression_hint: Invariant a correct fix must enforce: for every zip entry, the canonicalized/normalized extraction target File must be a descendant of the canonicalized destination directory (`dir`) before ANY filesystem operation (mkdirs, FileOutputStream, setLastModified) is performed on it; if it is not, extraction of that entry must be rejected (throw) rather than silently clamped, redirected, or skipped-but-continuing to process other sinks with the same unchecked path. The check must be applied once at/near Expand.java:153 (right after `resolveFile`) so it covers all four sinks (164/169/178/204) rather than patching only the FileOutputStream call — a partial fix that only guards line 178 would still leave directory-creation (164/169) and timestamp-tampering (204) exploitable. Known bypass variants the fix must also block: (a) simple parent traversal `../foo` (this POV) and multi-segment `../../../foo`; (b) traversal disguised as a directory entry (`../evilDir/`) that only hits the mkdirs sinks (164/169), not the write sink; (c) absolute-path entry names (e.g. `/etc/passwd` or on Windows `C:\...`), which `FileUtils.resolveFile` explicitly special-cases as root-relative absolute paths (FileUtils.java ~1378-1394) and would bypass a naive "startsWith(dest)" check if resolveFile itself isn't also constrained; (d) backslash-encoded traversal (`..\\foo`) since resolveFile normalizes separators; (e) symlink-based escapes where an entry name is benign but a pre-existing symlink inside dest points outside — canonicalization (getCanonicalPath) rather than mere string-prefix comparison on the absolute path is needed to catch this; (f) zip-slip via entries that differ only in case or trailing slashes on case-insensitive filesystems. A regression test should assert both that `../pwned.txt`-style entries are rejected/contained AND that a benign entry like `sub/dir/file.txt` still extracts normally inside dest.
parsed_output.summary: Created a runnable Java POV demonstrating CWE-22 "Zip Slip" in org.codehaus.plexus.util.Expand: a crafted zip entry named "../pwned.txt" causes Expand#extractFile() to write a file one directory above the intended destination via the public Expand.setSrc/setDest/execute() API, because FileUtils.resolveFile(dir, entryName) never validates that the resolved File stays inside dir.

parsed_output.patch_notes:
Root cause: Expand.java:153 built the extraction target `File f = FileUtils.resolveFile(dir, entryName)` purely from the attacker-controlled ZipEntry name (ze.getName(), line 116), with no post-resolution containment check. That single unchecked `f` then flowed into four sinks in extractFile(): dirF.mkdirs() (164), f.mkdirs() for directory entries (169), new FileOutputStream(f) (178), and f.setLastModified() (204).

Fix: added a single guard right after the resolveFile() call, before the try block's first filesystem operation, that canonicalizes both the destination directory and the resolved entry path (File#getCanonicalPath()) and rejects (throws IOException, wrapped by the existing `throws Exception` on extractFile) any entry whose canonical path is not equal to, or does not start with, the canonical destination directory (with a trailing separator to prevent sibling-prefix false negatives like `dest-evil` matching `dest`). Because the check sits once at the trust boundary (immediately after resolveFile, before any of the four sinks), it uniformly blocks:
  - simple/multi-segment `../` traversal (the POV's `../pwned.txt`)
  - traversal disguised as a directory entry (`../evilDir/`), which only hits the mkdirs sinks
  - absolute-path entries and backslash-encoded traversal, since resolveFile's output is still canonicalized and compared
  - symlink-based escapes, since getCanonicalPath() resolves symlinks rather than doing a plain string prefix check on the raw path

Benign nested entries (e.g. `sub/dir/file.txt`) still resolve inside dest and extract normally, since their canonical path naturally starts with the canonical dest path.

Added src/test/java/org/codehaus/plexus/util/ExpandTest.java (JUnit 3, consistent with the existing FileBasedTestCase-based test style) with three regression tests: (1) a `../pwned.txt` file entry is rejected and no file lands outside dest, (2) a `../evilDir/` directory entry is rejected and no directory is created outside dest, (3) a benign `sub/dir/file.txt` entry still extracts correctly with the right content inside dest.
parsed_output.risk_notes: Low risk. The change only adds a containment check on the resolved path before any extraction side effect occurs — it does not alter behavior for entries that resolve inside the destination directory (the common/benign case), which is covered by the added benign-entry regression test and the pre-existing FileUtilsTest/full suite (303/303 passing after the change). Extraction of a malicious/traversal entry now throws instead of silently succeeding or silently skipping — this is an intentional behavior change (fail-closed) per the alert's regression_hint, and is the correct semantics for a security fix (callers relying on Expand to safely extract untrusted archives will now get a clear failure instead of silent filesystem corruption outside the destination). Only two files touched: the source fix in Expand.java and a new, additive test file; no dependency, build, or unrelated code changes.
parsed_output.summary: Fixed CWE-22 Zip Slip in org.codehaus.plexus.util.Expand#extractFile by validating that the resolved extraction target stays within the destination directory immediately after FileUtils.resolveFile(dir, entryName), before any filesystem operation is performed on it.

parsed_output.summary: The patch adds a single containment check in Expand.extractFile() immediately after FileUtils.resolveFile(dir, entryName), before any filesystem operation. It canonicalizes both the destination directory and the resolved entry path and rejects (throws IOException) any entry whose canonical path is not equal to or does not start with the canonical destination path (with trailing separator to avoid sibling-prefix false negatives). This single guard sits before all four sinks identified in the alert (dirF.mkdirs() at 164, f.mkdirs() at 169, FileOutputStream(f) at 178, f.setLastModified() at 204), fully covering the reported CWE-22 Zip Slip trace. A new ExpandTest.java adds regression tests for a malicious file entry, a malicious directory entry, and a benign nested entry. I independently reran the POV against the patched worktree via the docker wrapper and confirmed it no longer reproduces (exits 1, prints SAFE, Expand.execute() throws as expected), and reran the regression suite (ExpandTest and the full `mvn test`), both passing (303/303 in the full suite, including the 3 new ExpandTest cases). The diff is minimal, targeted at the root cause, does not touch or weaken the POV, and does not remove any legitimate functionality — benign nested-path extraction still works.
